about: Zipacna follows the boys to the foot of the ravine under the mountain Meauan, where the false crab lies on its side, its back showing red. Starving, he tries to go in face down, and the crab climbs away upward; he comes out, then goes back in on his back, as the boys had told him, until only his knees show, and the great mountain comes down on his chest. He never comes out again: Zipacna becomes stone, the second of the proud ones brought low. Then a new section: the third, Cabracan, the second son of Vucub Caquix, who calls himself the destroyer of mountains. Huracan, Youngest Thunderbolt and Green Thunderbolt send the boys against him, telling them to lead him away to the east. They find him shaking down mountains, pass themselves off as poor nameless hunters, and tell him of a great mountain in the east that rises above all the others. He wants to see it and bring it down. Walking on either side of him, they shoot birds with their breath alone, and they roast one coated with white earth; its smell makes Cabracan's mouth water, and he begs for it and eats it. At the mountain the earth has taken his strength, and he can do nothing to the mountains. The boys bind his arms behind his back and his neck and legs together, throw him down and bury him. The part ends by saying that the downfall of Vucub Caquix, Zipacna and Cabracan has now been told, and that the birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque comes next.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xꜭha curi Zipacna, ta xbe cut achbilan chicut ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” he-said then Zipacna, then he-went then accompanying again-then the Zipacna.
sentences.i: “Very well,” said Zipacna, and he went along with them.
sentences.n: The part opens on Zipacna's answer to the boys' advice at the end of the last part, to go in on his back. Vꜩ bala 'very well', the house rendering. achbilan 'in company, going along with': taken as the ach 'companion' of rach 'together with' (first part), with -bil and -an (inferred; the modern rachb'il 'with him' is of this root); Brasseur 'de compagnie avec eux'. chicut is chic 'again' + cut 'then' written as one word, the c shared (toggle chik'ut); it comes back often in this part. Zipacna is named twice in the one sentence, as the text has it.

sentences.t: Xbec, xeopon chuxe zivan; ꜩalam cula ri tap, cacvacavoh vla rih;
sentences.l: He-went, they-arrived at-foot ravine; sideways(?) cula(?) the crab, glowing-red(?) hither its-back;
sentences.i: He went, and they came to the foot of the ravine. The crab lay there on its side, its back turned towards them, deep red;
sentences.n: Xbec 'he went' (be 'go' + -c), then xeopon 'they arrived': x- + e- 'they' + opon 'arrive (there)', the singular for Zipacna, the plural for all of them. chuxe zivan 'at the foot of the ravine', as in the last part. ꜩalam cula ri tap is read with Brasseur ('l'écrevisse était couchée de côté'): ꜩalam 'sideways, on its side' and cula 'it lies' are both inferred; neither is otherwise known. cacvacavoh is a doubled word of colour, after Brasseur's 'présentant une superficie fort rouge' (his cakvacavoh); his k stands for q, and the toggle gives kaq 'red' in the first syllable, an inference. Ximénez writes plain c, printed as written. vla rih 'hither its back': rih is r- 'its' + ih 'back', as in chirih 'behind it'.

sentences.t: xe zivan ri cute qui cumaꜩih.
sentences.l: foot ravine the then their cumaꜩih(?).
sentences.i: and there at the foot of the ravine lay their trick.
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb: xe zivan 'the foot of the ravine' is where the boys' qui cumaꜩih was. The word is not otherwise known. Brasseur renders it 'leur enchantement'; its letters are those of cumaꜩ 'serpent' (in Ꜫucumaꜩ) with -ih, and 'their trick, their contrivance' is a guess. cute 'then, so', the longer form of cut.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” chi quicot curi Zipacna, “car ahtah xcoc ta pu chi!”
sentences.l: “Good bala,” in joy then Zipacna, “he-wants(?) (tah) it-went-in (ta) in mouth!”
sentences.i: “Very well,” said Zipacna gladly. “If only it were in the mouth already!”
sentences.n: chi quicot 'in gladness': chi + quicot 'be glad', with no verb of saying. car ahtah xcoc ta pu chi is divided as the established text has it (MS tapuchi, divided ta pu chi); Brasseur reads ca r'ah-tah x-c'oc-tà pu chi, 'je voudrais qu'elle se trouvât déjà dans ma bouche'. Taken so: car is not car 'fish' but c- (ongoing) + r- 'he', run onto ah 'want', with tah, the particle of wishing; xcoc 'that it went in', from oc 'enter' (Brasseur x-c'oc; the role of its c is not clear; compare vcoc 'its going in' in the sixth part); pu chi 'in the mouth', chi 'mouth' (toggle chi'), pu as pa 'in' (inferred). The r- 'he' is third person, so the wish may be the narrator's ('he wished it were in his mouth') inside the speech marks; inferred. The English says 'the mouth' to leave this open.

sentences.t: Rumal quiꜩih cuꜩin chi vaih.
sentences.l: Because truly he-is-finished from hunger.
sentences.i: For truly he was perishing with hunger.
sentences.n: cuꜩin 'he is at an end': c- (ongoing) + vꜩin 'be finished' (from vꜩ 'good, complete'), as in the last part; Brasseur 'il se mourait de faim'. chi vaih 'of hunger': vaih is the word for hunger of the last part, where he had gone two days without eating; here no 'my' is meant.

sentences.t: Xrah cu tih ri; xa xrah hupunic, xrah oquic; pacal curi tap xacanic.
sentences.l: He-wanted then try(-it) the; only he-wanted face-down(?), he-wanted entering; upward(?) then the-crab it-climbed.
sentences.i: He wanted to try for it: he wanted to go in face down, he wanted to go in; but the crab climbed upward.
sentences.n: xrah 'he wanted', three times, with the action wanted after it. tih 'try', as in the second and fourth parts, its ti written with the ß-ligature (the same letters can be tij 'eat', as chi tihic later in this part; Brasseur 'tenter'); ri after it is unexplained. xa xrah hupunic: the MS has rixa xrah, divided ri xa xrah with Brasseur. hupunic 'face down' (inferred) is the hupulic of the last part with n for l, the posture in which the crab bit the boys. pacal is the pacalic 'face up' of the last part without -ic; here, beside xacanic 'it climbed', it reads as 'upward'. xacanic (MS xa|canic across the line, one word with Brasseur's x-akanic) is acan 'climb' with x- and -ic. Ximénez writes plain c in pacal and xacanic (Brasseur pagal, x-akanic), printed as written. Brasseur renders hupunic 'à plat ventre' and the pacal of his second going-in the same ('à plat ventre de nouveau'), while here he gives pacal curi tap xacanic only as 'l'écrevisse s'étant mise en marche en montant'; the opposition 'face down' / 'face up' is kept from the last part, inferred.

sentences.t: Cate cut xel chu vloc.
sentences.l: Then then he-came-out chu hither.
sentences.i: Then he came back out.
sentences.n: xel 'he went out', with vloc 'hither': he came out towards the boys. chu is not clear here (perhaps chi + v- 'at its', the mouth of the cave); left unrendered.

sentences.t: “Maui xa rico?” xuꜭhax cut.
sentences.l: “Not you-did find-it?” he-was-told then.
sentences.i: “Haven't you got it?” they asked him.
sentences.n: xa rico 'you found it', with Brasseur's x-a riqo: x- + a- 'you' + rico 'find', as in the earlier parts. It is not xa 'only', though the letters are the same. xuꜭhax 'he was told', the passive of ꜭha 'say', as in the last part.

sentences.t: “Mahabi; xa pacalic cacanic; xa nabe zcaquin chic maui mi xnu rico.
sentences.l: “Not-yet; only upward(?) it-climbs; only first a-little(?) more not just I-found-it.
sentences.i: “Not yet; it just keeps climbing upward. I came within a little of getting it.
sentences.n: cacanic 'it climbs, it is climbing': c- (ongoing) + acan 'climb' + -ic, the verb of xacanic. pacalic is the word of the last part, here with the climbing verb: 'upward', inferred, as pacal above. xa nabe zcaquin chic maui mi xnu rico 'only at first, a little more, I did not get it', that is, he nearly had it: the same turn as the boys' own in the last part (xa cu zcaquin chic maui chi ca rico). xnu rico 'I found it': x- + nu- 'I' + rico. zcaquin 'a little' is inferred.

sentences.t: Cate vꜩlo qui paqueic quin oc vbic,” xꜭha chicut.
sentences.l: Then good-perhaps qui face-up(?) I-go-in thither,” he-said again-then.
sentences.i: Perhaps it would be better if I went in on my back,” he said.
sentences.n: vꜩlo is vꜩ 'good' + lo 'perhaps', written as one word (Brasseur utz-lo; his French 'peut-être serait-il bon que j'entrasse'). paqueic is not otherwise known, and Brasseur leaves it out of his French. Its letters begin like pacal and pacalic, and in the next sentence he goes in pacal, so it is taken as 'face up, on the back', the posture the boys advised; a guess. qui before it is unexplained. quin oc vbic 'I go in thither': quin is c- + in 'I'.

sentences.t: Cate cut pacal chic ta xoc vbic.
sentences.l: Then then face-up(?) now when he-went-in thither.
sentences.i: So then he went in again, this time on his back.
sentences.n: pacal chic 'face up now': he goes in as the boys told him (inferred; Brasseur 'à plat ventre de nouveau', taking the posture as the same as before). Ximénez writes plain c (Brasseur pagal); printed as written. xoc vbic 'he went in thither'.

sentences.t: Xquiz cu oc vbic; xa v vi vchec chic xcutun vloc.
sentences.l: It-finished then entering thither; only its top his-knees(?) now it-appeared hither.
sentences.i: He went all the way in; only the tops of his knees could still be seen.
sentences.n: Xquiz cu oc vbic 'it was finished, the going in': xquiz 'it ended', as in the earlier parts. v vi vchec 'its top, his chec' (divided so in the established text): vi here is the noun 'head, top' (toggle wi'). vchec is v- 'his' + chec, after Brasseur 'il ne montrait plus que l'extrémité de ses jambes'; the modern ch'ek 'knee' would fit, but the ejective is not restored (toggle uchek), and 'knees' is inferred. xcutun 'it showed, appeared': the verb of vcutunizaxic 'its being shown' in the first part (toggle k'utun).

sentences.t: Xquiz biquitahic, xtilob cu cahoc nima huyub chi vꜭux;
sentences.l: It-finished biquitahic(?), it-xtilob(?) then downward great mountain on his-heart;
sentences.i: The great mountain broke loose and came down upon his chest;
sentences.n: Both verbs are doubtful, and the English follows Brasseur ('la grande montagne, minée par en bas, achevant de se détacher vint couvrir sa poitrine'), a guess. biquitahic, a passive noun in -tah-ic, is not otherwise known; 'its loosening' is inferred from Brasseur. xtilob: the image has x + a tall looped letter + i + lob, read with the ti ligature as in the earlier parts (it could be xhilob); Brasseur's word is garbled in the OCR (х-Шор), and the meaning is unknown; 'came down' is guessed from cahoc 'downward'. chi vꜭux 'on his heart, his chest': the letter is q-shaped, read ꜭ with Brasseur (u qux). The mountain is Meauan, where the boys hid the false crab in the last part.

sentences.t: maui xꜩolcopih chic; abah cut xuxic ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: not he-turned-back again; stone then became the Zipacna.
sentences.i: he did not come back out again, and Zipacna became stone.
sentences.n: xꜩolcopih 'he turned back': taken with Brasseur ('il ne retourna plus') as a form of ꜩol 'return' (modern tzolij); the ending -copih is not otherwise known. abah cut xuxic 'stone then he became': xuxic 'became', as in the earlier parts, with abah 'stone' put first for weight.

sentences.t: Quehe vchacatahic chic Zipacna cumal ꜭaholab Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Thus his-being-brought-low in-turn Zipacna by-them boys Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Such was the overthrow of Zipacna in his turn, at the hands of the boys Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: vchacatahic 'his being brought low', the word of the last two parts: v- 'his' + chacatah 'be overcome' + -ic. chic 'in turn', for Vucub Caquix went first. cumal 'by them', the 3rd-person plural of rumal.

sentences.t: Ri banol huyub, xꜭha v ꜩihoxic oher, v nabe ꜭahol Vvcub Caquix, chuxe huyub Meauan vbi xchacatah vi.
sentences.l: The maker mountain, said its being-told of-old, its first son Seven Macaw, at-foot mountain Meauan its-name he-was-brought-low there.
sentences.i: He, the maker of mountains, so the ancient telling says, the first son of Vucub Caquix, was brought low at the foot of the mountain called Meauan.
sentences.n: banol huyub 'maker of mountains': banol is the agent noun of ban 'make' (-ol); in the fifth part Zipacna's play is with the great mountains. xꜭha v ꜩihoxic oher 'the old telling said': the account itself is the speaker. v nabe ꜭahol 'his first son'. xchacatah vi 'he was brought low there', the passive verb, vi pointing back to the place. Meauan: the name of the mountain, its meaning not known; Brasseur, in a note, puts it on the Chixoy river, about eight leagues west of Rabinal.

sentences.t: Xa naual xchacatah vi v cab nimarizai rib.
sentences.l: Only spirit-power he-was-brought-low there its second making-great(?) himself.
sentences.i: Only by spirit power was he brought low, the second of those who made themselves great.
sentences.n: v cab 'its second' (written apart, as the established text divides it, against vcab 'his hand' at the end of this part): Zipacna is the second of the proud ones, Vucub Caquix being the first, though he is the first son. nimarizai rib 'the one who makes himself great', the phrase of the fifth part. naual 'spirit power' (house rendering): the boys won by it, not by force.

sentences.t: Hun chicut xchi ca biyh vbixic.
sentences.l: One again-then shall we tell its-telling.
sentences.i: Now we shall tell the story of one more.
sentences.n: Hun chicut 'one more, then': chic + cut as one word. xchi ca biyh 'we shall tell': xchi 'shall' + ca 'we' + biyh 'say, tell'. The MS writes byh with a small mark above the y; it is printed biyh as in the earlier parts (the same at bochiyh, qui biyh and mi xca biyh below). vbixic 'its being told'.

sentences.t: Rox chicut nimarizai rib, v cab vꜭahol Vvcub Caquix, Cabrracan vbi. “In yohol huiub,” xꜭha.
sentences.l: Its-third again-then making-great(?) himself, its second his-son Seven Macaw, Cabracan his-name. “I undoer mountain,” he-said.
sentences.i: The third who made himself great was the second son of Vucub Caquix, Cabracan by name. “I am the destroyer of mountains,” he said.
sentences.n: A new section begins here in the manuscript, with a large R. Rox 'its third' (r- 'its' + ox 'three'): Cabracan is the third of the proud ones and v cab vꜭahol 'his second son'. The name is written Cabrracan with rr here and in six other places in this part, Cabracan with one r in seven; both are printed as written, the toggle keeps the letters, and the English has Cabracan (its meaning is not certain; Brasseur, in a note, takes his answer below as a figure of the almost constant earthquakes of the region). yohol 'one who undoes, destroys': an agent noun in -ol, taken from yoh 'undo, knock down' (modern yojik; inferred). In … huiub has no verb 'to be', which K'iche' leaves out; huiub is huyub 'mountain' written with i.

sentences.t: Xavi cu xere Hunahpu, Xbalanque xchacou re Cabrracan.
sentences.l: Just then only-these Hunahpu, Xbalanque did-the-overcoming of Cabracan.
sentences.i: And again it was Hunahpu and Xbalanque alone who overcame Cabracan.
sentences.n: xavi … xere 'just these, these alone': the same two boys again. xchacou re 'they did the overcoming of him': the MS writes xchacoure, divided with Brasseur (x-chakou re). chacou is taken as the chac of xchac 'he was beaten' in the last part, with the -ou of a verb that names the doers, as in xbanouic 'were the ones who did it' in the sixth part; re 'of' then carries Cabracan. Inferred.

sentences.t: Xꜭha ri Huracan, Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha, ta xꜭhauic chiquech ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque:
sentences.l: He-said the Huracan, Youngest Thunderbolt, Green Thunderbolt, when he-spoke to-them the Hunahpu, Xbalanque:
sentences.i: Huracan, Youngest Thunderbolt and Green Thunderbolt spoke, and said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque:
sentences.n: The three of the Heart of Sky named in the first part speak with a singular verb (xꜭha, xꜭhauic), as one. ri before Huracan: at the head of image 0031 the first word is heavily inked; it is read ri with Brasseur. xꜭhauic chiquech 'he spoke to them': ꜭhau 'speak' + -ic, chiquech 'to them'.

sentences.t: “V cab vꜭahol Vvcub Caquix hunchic, hunchic chi chacatahic;
sentences.l: “Its second his-son Seven Macaw one-more, one-more that being-brought-low;
sentences.i: “The second son of Vucub Caquix: one more, let one more be brought low;
sentences.n: hunchic 'one more' (hun 'one' + chic), said twice. chi chacatahic 'that (he) be brought low': chi before the verbal noun, as a command or a wish. v cab 'the second', as above.

sentences.t: xavi nu ꜩih, rumal maui vꜩ qui banoh chuvach vleuh, ca qui couizah ꜫih chi nimal, chi alal; ma cu quehe chuxic.
sentences.l: just my word, because not good their doing on-the-face-of earth, ongoing they make-strong(?) day in greatness, in weight; not then thus it-shall-be.
sentences.i: this too is my word: for what they do on the face of the earth is not good; they exalt their day to greatness, to weight. It shall not be so.
sentences.n: xavi nu ꜩih 'this too is my word', that is, my will. ca qui couizah ꜫih 'they make their day strong, they raise it up': couizah is taken as cou 'strong, hard' + -izah 'make' (inferred; Brasseur 'd'exalter leur gloire'). His qu'iqouizah has q, his letter for ꜭ; the MS has plain c, and here a plain z with a heavy bar, not the ligature; printed as written. ꜫih 'day' is their day of fortune, as vꜫih Vucub Caquix 'his day' in the fifth part. nimal 'greatness' and alal 'weight' (al 'heavy' + -al) are the couplet. ma cu quehe chuxic 'it shall not be so then'.

sentences.t: Chi bochiyh cu vbic chila relebal ꜫih,” xꜭha cut ri Huracan chique ri e caib ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: You(pl.)-coax-him then thither there its-going-out-place sun,” he-said then the Huracan to-them the (e) two boys.
sentences.i: Coax him away, over there to where the sun comes out,” Huracan said to the two boys.
sentences.n: bochiyh 'coax, lead on with words', after Brasseur ('attirez-le avec douceur'), inferred; the MS has bochyh with a mark above the y, printed bochiyh as biyh. chi is ch- (command) + i- 'you (pl.)'. cu is written above the line over bochyh (Brasseur Ch'y bochiyh cu ubic) and printed in place. relebal ꜫih 'the sun's going-out place', the east: r- 'its' + el 'go out' + -ebal (place) + ꜫih 'sun' (a q-shaped letter where Brasseur has g, read ꜫ).

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala, lal ahau; que vi na cut. Maui vꜩ vi ca quilo.
sentences.l: “Good bala, you(sir) lord; thus there now then. Not good there we we-see.
sentences.i: “Very well, my lord; so be it. What we see is not good.
sentences.n: lal ahau 'my lord' (house rendering), lal being the respectful 'you'. que vi na cut 'so then': que 'thus' + vi + na, an assent; inferred. ca quilo 'we see': ca 'we' with quilo (q- 'we' + il 'see' + -o), the 'we' marked twice, as Brasseur prints ka kilo (his k is q).

sentences.t: Ma pa lal ꜭolic, lal pu yacalic, lal Vꜭux Cah?” xeꜭha cut ri ꜭaholab, ta xqui culuba vꜩih Huracan.
sentences.l: Not (pa) you(sir) existing, you(sir) also standing-up, you(sir) Heart of-Sky?” they-said then the boys, when they received(?) his-word Huracan.
sentences.i: Are you not the one who is, the one who stands, you, Heart of Sky?” said the boys, as they accepted Huracan's word.
sentences.n: ꜭolic, yacalic 'existing, standing up' are the pair of the first part (xma ꜭovi naquila ꜭolic, yacalic 'nothing existed, nothing stood upright'): the boys answer the god in the words of the creation. Ma pa … ? asks a question. The q-shaped letter of Vꜭux is read ꜭ with Brasseur (Lal u Qux cah). xqui culuba vꜩih 'they received his word': culuba is taken as a verb of receiving, meeting, the cul of xculutah 'he was met' below; Brasseur 'en écoutant'; inferred.

sentences.t: Are puch ca tahin ri Cabrracan iohol huyub;
sentences.l: This also ongoing busy the Cabracan destroying mountain;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Cabracan was busy destroying mountains;
sentences.n: ca tahin 'he is at it, busy': tahin, the word of the modern progressive tajin 'in the act of', here with ca (ongoing); Brasseur 'occupé à remuer les montagnes'. iohol is written with i here, yohol elsewhere; printed as written, the toggle yojol, as huiub gives juyub'.

sentences.t: xa zcaquin chutinih racan chuvach vleuh, huzu chi bulih nima huiub, chuti huyub rumal.
sentences.l: only a-little(?) he-chutinih(?) his-leg on-the-face-of earth, at-once (chi) crumble(?) great mountain, small mountain by-him.
sentences.i: he had only to tap his foot a little on the face of the earth, and at once the great mountains and the small mountains fell to pieces because of him.
sentences.n: chutinih is not clear: chu- 'he' (ch- + v-) + tinih, or a word made from chuti 'small'; its ti, like that of chuti, is written with the ß-ligature. 'Tap, stamp' follows Brasseur ('pour si peu qu'il battait des pieds') and is a guess. racan 'his leg, his foot'. bulih 'crumble, tear apart' is inferred from Brasseur ('se déchiraient'). huzu chi 'at once': huzu as in the second part (toggle jusuk). nima huiub, chuti huyub 'the great mountains, the small mountains', written once with i and once with y.

sentences.t: Ta xculutah cumal ri ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Then he-was-met by-them the boys.
sentences.i: Then the boys came upon him.
sentences.n: xculutah 'he was met': cul 'meet' + -utah, a passive (inferred; Brasseur 'il fut rencontré'). cumal ri ꜭaholab 'by the boys'.

sentences.t: “Apa cat be vi, at ꜭahol?” xeꜭha chirech ri Cabracan.
sentences.l: “Where you go there, you boy?” they-said to-him the Cabracan.
sentences.i: “Where are you going, boy?” they said to Cabracan.
sentences.n: Apa … vi 'where': apa asks the place and vi points back to it. cat be 'you are going': c- (ongoing) + at 'you' + be 'go'. at ꜭahol 'you, boy', the address between young men of the last part.

sentences.t: “Mahabi quin be vi; xa in vliy huyub; in puch yohol rech chi be ꜫih, chi be zac,” xꜭha cut, ta xꜭhauic.
sentences.l: “Nowhere I go there; only I bringing-down mountain; I also undoer of-it as-long-as goes sun, as-long-as goes light,” he-said then, when he-spoke.
sentences.i: “I am going nowhere; I am only bringing down the mountains. I am their destroyer for as long as the sun goes, for as long as the light goes,” he said in answer.
sentences.n: Mahabi … vi 'nowhere': the negative 'there is not' with the place word. vliy 'bringing down': the MS writes vly with a small i above, printed vliy with Brasseur (uliy); the verb of vlih in Cabracan's boast in the fifth part (chin vlih ronohel vleu). rech 'of it', of the mountains. chi be ꜫih, chi be zac 'while the sun goes, while the light goes': a couplet for 'always' (Brasseur's note: 'sans cesse, toujours').

sentences.t: Xꜭha chicut ri Cabrracan chique ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “Hupacha xpetic? Maui vetaam vvach. Naquipa ibi?” xꜭha Cabrracan.
sentences.l: He-said again-then the Cabracan to-them the Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “How you-came? Not I-know its-face. What your(pl.)-name?” he-said Cabracan.
sentences.i: Then Cabracan said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque: “How is it you have come? I do not know your faces. What are your names?” said Cabracan.
sentences.n: Hupacha xpetic 'how did (you) come?': pet 'come' + -ic, the person not marked. vetaam 'I know' (v- 'I' + etaam), as in the last part. vvach 'its face': the face before him (Brasseur 'je ne connais pas ce visage'). ibi 'your (pl.) name': i- 'your (pl.)' + bi 'name'.

sentences.t: “Mahabi ca bi; xa oh vbom, xa pu oh ꜩarabom pa tac huyub;
sentences.l: “There-is-not our name; only we blowgunners, only also we bird-limers(?) in (tac) mountain;
sentences.i: “We have no name; we are only blowgunners, only bird-limers in the mountains;
sentences.n: ca bi 'our name' (MS cabi, divided with Brasseur, ka bi). vbom 'blowgunners': vb 'blowgun' + -om, the one who does it; ꜩarabom, its pair, 'bird-limers', after Brasseur's note ('nous chassant au glu'), inferred. The boys hide who they are. pa tac huyub 'among the mountains': tac marks the plural, as in the last part.

sentences.t: xa oh meba, mahabi naquila quech, at ꜭahol.
sentences.l: only we orphans, there-is-not anything ours, you boy.
sentences.i: we are only orphans, with nothing of our own, boy.
sentences.n: meba 'poor, orphaned' (modern meb'a', the word certain; Brasseur 'orphelins'). naquila quech 'anything of ours': quech 'ours', q- + ech.

sentences.t: Xa chuti huyub, xa nima huyub coh bec, at ꜭahol.
sentences.l: Only small mountain, only great mountain we-go, you boy.
sentences.i: We just go about the small mountains and the great mountains, boy.
sentences.n: coh bec 'we go': c- (ongoing) + oh 'we' + bec, be 'go' with -ec, as in the last part. The small and the great mountains are the couplet of Cabracan's stamping above, turned to their wandering.

sentences.t: Are curi hun nima huyub xquilo; xa co quil caquiye;
sentences.l: This then one great mountain we-saw; only there-is seen(?) caquiye(?);
sentences.i: But we have seen one great mountain; there it stands, and great cliffs are to be seen;
sentences.n: xquilo 'we saw': the toggle gives q- 'we' (Brasseur x-K'ilo, his k is q), where xquilo is 'they saw' (xkilo) in the earlier parts; the speakers here are the boys. xa co quil caquiye is not clear: co is ꜭo 'there is' written with plain c (Brasseur qo, his letter for ꜭ), printed as the image has it; quil may be 'it is seen' (il 'see'); caquiye (Brasseur cakiye) is not otherwise known. Brasseur's French has 'où elle est on voit de grands précipices', and the English follows him; a guess.

sentences.t: quiꜩih naht cacanic, xa ca cupupic qui couic chuvi huyub ronohel.
sentences.l: truly far it-climbs, only ongoing it-rises(?) so(?) passing on-top-of mountain all.
sentences.i: truly it climbs high, it rises clear above the tops of all the mountains.
sentences.n: naht cacanic 'it climbs far': cacanic, the climbing verb of the crab above, now of the mountain (Brasseur 'elle s'élève à une grande hauteur'). cupupic 'rising' is inferred from Brasseur ('elle surpasse les cimes de toutes les montagnes'). qui couic is taken as qui 'so' + couic 'passing', the verb of xe icouic 'they passed' in the sixth part; Brasseur's qu'iqovic has q, but Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle respells the letters (kowik), the reading being inferred. chuvi huyub ronohel 'above all the mountains'.

sentences.t: Ma cu habi hun caib ꜩiquin mi xca cam chuvach, at ꜭahol.
sentences.l: Not then there-is one two bird just-now we-took before-it, you boy.
sentences.i: And not one bird, not two, have we taken in front of it, boy.
sentences.n: Ma cu habi 'there was not' (MS macuhabi). hun caib 'one, two', that is, not a single one. mi xca cam 'we have taken' (MS mixcacam, divided mi xca cam): x- + ca 'we' + cam 'take'; Brasseur ka qam, his q being the letter of ꜭ, so the toggle shows k'am, as xquicam in the fifth and sixth parts. chuvach 'before it', the mountain: it spoils their hunting, so the boys say; the bait for Cabracan is the mountain itself.

sentences.t: Ve cut quiꜩih ca vulih ronohel huiub, at ꜭahol?” xeꜭha ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque chire Cabrracan.
sentences.l: If then truly you-bring-down all mountain, you boy?” they-said the Hunahpu, Xbalanque to-him Cabracan.
sentences.i: Is it true, then, that you bring down all the mountains, boy?” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque to Cabracan.
sentences.n: Ve … ? 'is it so that …?': ve 'if, whether' makes the question. ca vulih 'you bring down': c- (ongoing) + av- 'you', its v run onto vlih (Brasseur c'av'ulih); the toggle respells the two words as written.

sentences.t: “Ma quiꜩih xivilo ri huiub qui biyh? Apa ꜭo vi? Xchi vil na, xchin vulih cahoc. Apa xivil vi?”
sentences.l: “Not truly you(pl.)-saw-it the mountain you(pl.)-say? Where is-it there? I-shall-see-it now, I-shall I-bring-it-down downward. Where you(pl.)-saw-it there?”
sentences.i: “Have you truly seen the mountain you speak of? Where is it? I shall see it, and I shall bring it down. Where did you see it?”
sentences.n: xivilo 'you (pl.) saw it': x- + iv- 'you (pl.)' (the form of i- before a vowel) + il 'see' + -o; xivil vi the same without -o, with vi 'there'. qui biyh 'you (pl.) say': c- (ongoing) + i- 'you (pl.)', written qui (MS quibyh, printed biyh as above). Xchi vil na 'I shall see it' (MS xchivilna; Brasseur K-chi vil na): xchi 'shall' + v- 'I' + il. xchin vulih 'I shall bring it down': xchin 'I shall' + v- 'I' + vlih, the 'I' marked twice; cahoc 'downward'.

sentences.t: “Chila ba ꜭo vi chi relebal ꜫih,” xeꜭha cut Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: “There (ba) it-is there at its-going-out-place sun,” they-said then Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: “It is over there, where the sun comes out,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: ba, the particle of urging of the last parts, here perhaps pointing ('over there, look'). chi relebal ꜫih 'at the sun's going-out place', the east, where Huracan told them to lead him.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ. Chi cama ca be,” xe vꜭhax cu ri e caib chi ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: “Good. You(pl.)-take our road,” they were-told then the (e) two (chi) boys.
sentences.i: “Good. Lead us on our way,” the two boys were told.
sentences.n: Chi cama ca be 'take our road' (MS chicama|cabe): chi is ch- + i- 'you (pl.)'; cama 'take', the word of the earlier parts, printed with plain c as the image has it and respelled kama in the toggle as there. Brasseur has Ch'y gama ka be, with g (his letter for ꜫ), and 'montrez-nous le chemin'; the sense 'lead the way' is inferred. Compare mi xca cam above, where he has q. xe vꜭhax 'they were told': xe 'they' + vꜭhax, the passive of ꜭha, as in the second part. e caib chi ꜭaholab 'the two boys', chi joining the number to the noun.

sentences.t: “Mahabi; xa ca chape nicah chi ca xol, cut ꜭohe vi hun cha mox, hun cha vi qui cab chique, rumal ꜭo ca vvb.
sentences.l: “No; only we take-you middle at our between, so-that be there one at-your left, one at-your right(?) of-us, because there-are our blowguns.
sentences.i: “No; we will just take you between us, in the middle, so that one of us is on your left and one on your right, for we have our blowguns.
sentences.n: ca chape 'we take (you)': chap 'catch, take hold', with -e (inferred). nicah 'the middle, the half' (modern nik'aj, the word certain, the ejective restored). chi ca xol 'between us' (MS chicaxol). hun cha mox, hun cha vi qui cab: cha is taken as chi + a- 'at your'; mox 'left'; vi qui cab, three words as the established text divides them, is taken as the modern wikiq'ab' 'right hand', with cab 'hand' in plain c (Brasseur qui gab, with g; the toggle q'ab' as cab 'hand' in an earlier part). This is inferred from the pair with mox and from Brasseur's 'à ta gauche … à ta droite'. chique 'of us' (Brasseur chike, his k is q). ꜭo ca vvb 'we have our blowguns', 'there are our blowguns'. After ca 'our' and qui 'their' Ximénez writes vvb (so qui vvb, ca vvbah, qui vvbanic below), and the toggle respells the two letters wu (wub'), as 007's ivvbah gave iwub'aj; whether the v is a glide or part of the prefix is not clear. vvb alone, 'his blowgun' (fifth part), was uub', its first v the u- 'his'.

sentences.t: Ve ꜭo ꜩiquin chi ca vvbah,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: If there-are birds that we-shoot-them,” they-said then.
sentences.i: If there are birds, we shall shoot them,” they said.
sentences.n: vvbah 'shoot with the blowgun', the verb of vb, as ivvbah in the last part; chi ca 'that we', here 'we shall'.

sentences.t: Que quicot chi qui tihtobela qui vvbanic.
sentences.l: They rejoice that they test their blowgunning.
sentences.i: They were glad as they tried out their blowguns.
sentences.n: que quicot 'they are glad': que is c- + e 'they' (ongoing). qui tihtobela 'they try out': the tihtobeh 'test' of the second part (tih 'try'), its ti written with the ß-ligature; the ending -ela is not otherwise known. qui vvbanic 'their blowgunning', a noun of vvbah.

sentences.t: Are curi ta que vvbanic, mana vleuh tah vbac qui vvb; xa chi cuxlabih ri ꜩiquin ta chi qui vvbah.
sentences.l: This then when they blowgun, not earth (tah) its-bone their blowgun; only (chi) they-breathe-on(?) the birds when (chi) they-shoot-them.
sentences.i: But when they shot, the pellets of their blowguns were not of clay; they only blew their breath at the birds when they shot them.
sentences.n: mana … tah 'not': the two parts of the negative, around vleuh 'earth'. vbac qui vvb 'the bone of their blowgun', that is, the pellet, made of clay as a rule (Brasseur 'balles de terre'). cuxlabih 'they breathe at': uxlab 'breath' (ruxlab below) made a verb with -ih; its c- is taken as 'they', the form of qui before a vowel (as calaxic at the end of this part), after chi; inferred, after Brasseur ('ils soufflaient'). Brasseur's note: they brought the birds down with their breath alone.

sentences.t: Chu maihah curi Cabracan.
sentences.l: He-marvels-at-it then Cabracan.
sentences.i: And Cabracan marvelled.
sentences.n: maihah 'wonder at, marvel', after Brasseur ('était émerveillé'), inferred. chu is taken as ch- + v- 'he' before the verb, without the sense 'let' it has elsewhere.

sentences.t: Ta xqui bac cu qui cac ri ꜭaholab; xqui bol cut qui ꜩiquin chuvach cac.
sentences.l: Then they drilled(?) then their fire the boys; they roasted then their birds before fire.
sentences.i: Then the boys kindled their fire, and they roasted their birds before the fire.
sentences.n: qui cac 'their fire': cac is ꜫaꜫ 'fire' written with plain c (Brasseur gag), the toggle q'aq' as in an earlier part; so also chuvach cac 'before the fire'. xqui bac 'they made (fire)': Brasseur has 'battirent du feu' ('struck fire'); the letters are those of bac 'bone', and the drilling of fire (a stick twirled on a board) is the drafter's guess, not his. xqui bol 'they roasted' (inferred; Brasseur 'mirent rôtir'), the verb of vbolic 'its roasting' below.

sentences.t: Hun cut ꜩiquin xqui cul zahcab chirih; zaqui vleu xqui coho.
sentences.l: One then bird they-coated white-earth(?) on-its-back; white earth they-put-it.
sentences.i: One bird they smeared with chalky earth; they put white earth all over it.
sentences.n: zahcab is the white earth that the next words call zaqui vleu 'white earth'; Brasseur 'du zizate', in his note Nahuatl tizatl, a whitish, very crumbly earth used to polish metals and make cement. The word is respelled as written (sajkab'); that it is a K'iche' word for lime is not shown. xqui cul 'they smeared, coated' (inferred; Brasseur 'frottèrent'). xqui coho 'they put it (on)': coh 'put' + -o. chirih 'on its back, over it'. The earth is the trick: it will take Cabracan's strength.

sentences.t: “Are cut chi ca ya chire ta hiconoc, ta chu ꜩica puch ruxlab.
sentences.l: “This then that we-give to-him when hiconoc(?), when it ꜩica(?) also its-breath.
sentences.i: “This is the one we shall give him, to rouse his appetite, when its smell reaches him.
sentences.n: chi ca ya chire 'that we give him': ya 'give'. ta hiconoc: the MS has chire tahiconoc, divided ta hiconoc with Brasseur (ta higon-oc); the word is not otherwise known and its meaning is unclear; 'to rouse his appetite' follows Brasseur's 'pour exciter son appétit', a guess. ta chu ꜩica puch ruxlab: ruxlab 'its breath, its smell' (r- + uxlab); ꜩica, with the plain ligature, is not otherwise known, and 'reach' is a guess from Brasseur's 'par le fumet qui en sortira'.

sentences.t: Ca ꜩiquin ta chacahoc.
sentences.l: Our bird let it-be-done(?).
sentences.i: Let our bird be cooked through.
sentences.n: chacahoc is taken as the verb of xchacah 'it cooked' below (Brasseur x-chagah, 'se cuisait'), with -oc, and ta as the particle of wishing; inferred. Brasseur divides ta ch'u kah-oc here, with k (his q) where xchacah has g, and reads 'cet oiseau doit être sa défaite', taking the cah of cahoc 'downward': so his letters do not support the link with xchacah, and the line is uncertain. ca 'our' (Brasseur ka).

sentences.t: Are curi vleuh xchoc chirih ꜩiquin cumal; puleu chi ca ꜩac vi, quehe cat puvleu chi muc vi.
sentences.l: This then earth it-shall-go-in on-its-back bird by-us; to-earth that we-drop-him there, thus (cat) in-earth that he-be-buried there.
sentences.i: As the earth goes onto the bird's back at our hands, so on the earth we shall bring him down, so in the earth he shall be buried.
sentences.n: xchoc 'it shall go (on)': xch- 'shall' + oc. cumal 'by us' here, the toggle q- (Brasseur kumal, his k is q), where cumal is 'by them' in the narrative. puleu, puvleu 'on the earth, in the earth': pa 'in' + vleu, written pu|leu and pu|vleu across the lines (Brasseur p'uleu both times), printed as written. chi ca ꜩac 'that we drop (him)', ꜩac 'fall, let fall'. chi muc vi 'that (he) be buried there': muc 'bury' (modern muq; Brasseur muk, his k is q). quehe cat 'so then': cat is taken as cut, Brasseur printing quehecut; the toggle respells the letters. The couplet says it: as the bird is wrapped in earth, so Cabracan.

sentences.t: Ve nima etamanel hun ꜩac, hun bit ta chanax oc, ta zaquir oc,” xeꜭha ri ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: If great knower one ꜩac, one shaped when it-is-sown(?), when it-dawns,” they-said the boys.
sentences.i: Great would be the knowing of one built, one shaped, when there is sowing, when there is dawn,” said the boys.
sentences.n: Brasseur calls this sentence obscure (his French: 'il est grand, il est sage (de penser à) former la créature, au moment où vont paraître les semailles et où le jour va se montrer'), and so it is; the English is a guess. hun ꜩac, hun bit 'one ꜩac, one shaped' echoes vinac ꜯac, vinac bit 'a person built, a person shaped' of the second part, though ꜩac has the plain ligature, as ꜩac 'drop' just before (Brasseur hun tzak); it is respelled as written. ta chanax oc, ta zaquir oc 'when it is sown, when it dawns' echoes ta chauaxoc, ta zaquiroc of the first and second parts; chanax is taken as chauax with n for v (inferred). The second z, in zaquir, is a plain z with a tail, not the ligature. etamanel 'one who knows, a sage' (first part). Ve 'if' is left out of the English.

sentences.t: “Rumal xax chi rain vi vꜭuxlal ri chi tihic, chi chacuxic, quehe xchu raih vꜭux ri Cabracan,” xeꜭha chi quibil quib Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: “Because truly that it-wants there the-heart the that eating, that chewing(?), thus it-shall want his-heart the Cabracan,” they-said among themselves themselves Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: “Just as the heart truly longs for eating, for chewing, so the heart of Cabracan will long for it,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque to each other.
sentences.n: rain 'it wants, it longs for' and raih in xchu raih 'it shall want' are taken as r- 'it' + ai(h) 'desire', as rraih below (inferred, after Brasseur's 'désirer' and 'convoite'). vꜭuxlal 'heart, inner self': ꜭux + -lal, here the heart of anyone; the letter is q-shaped, read ꜭ with Brasseur (u quxlal), and so in vꜭux. chi tihic, chi chacuxic 'eating, chewing' are both doubtful. In tihic a heavy blot sits on the ligature; it is read tih, the letters of tih 'try' above, here 'eat' (modern tij 'eat'), and Brasseur's word is garbled in the OCR (бус). In chacuxic the image has a small c before hacuxic, where Brasseur prints hakuxic; 'chewing' follows his 'broyer sous la dent', a guess. chi quibil quib 'among themselves'.

sentences.t: Ta xqui bol ri ꜩiquin; xchacah cut ꜫan vbolic, chi yipouic, chi cabchiyanic quih ri ꜩiquin, chi coinic zimizoh ruxlab.
sentences.l: Then they roasted the bird; it-cooked(?) then yellow its-roasting, (chi) turning(?), (chi) dripping(?) its-juice(?) the bird, (chi) strong(?) savoury its-smell.
sentences.i: Then they roasted the bird, and it cooked to yellow in the roasting, turning, the bird's juices dripping, its savoury smell strong.
sentences.n: Much here is inferred from Brasseur's French ('l'oiseau qui se cuisait et prenait couleur en tournant, le jus de l'oiseau ruisselant de toutes parts avec sa graisse qui exhalait le fumet le plus appétissant'). xchacah 'it cooked' (Brasseur x-chagah, with g; the MS plain c, respelled). ꜫan 'yellow', written with the tresillo (Brasseur gan). vbolic 'its roasting', the noun of bol. chi yipouic: MS chiyipo|uic, read y-i-p; doubtful, and 'turning' is a guess. chi cabchiyanic quih: cabchiyanic (Brasseur's print cabehiyanic) 'dripping' and quih 'its juice', written qu + i as Brasseur's quih and kept, not ꜫih; both inferred. coinic 'strongly' is taken from cou 'strong', a guess. zimizoh 'savoury, fragrant', the word of vzimzohil below.

sentences.t: Are curi Cabrracan cu rraih chic rechaxic;
sentences.l: This then Cabracan he wants now its-eating;
sentences.i: And now Cabracan longed to eat it;
sentences.n: cu rraih 'he wants it': cu is c- + v- 'he' (ongoing), rraih the r- + aih 'desire' of rain above, its r doubled in the MS (Brasseur c'u raih); printed as written. rechaxic 'its eating': r- 'its' + echa 'food' + -x- + -ic, as in the last part.

sentences.t: xa cauahin vvaal pu chi, xa cabiquilahic, ca curulah puch vchub, vcaxah rumal vzimzohil ꜩiquin.
sentences.l: only it-flows(?) its-water in mouth, only he-gapes(?), ongoing it-runs(?) also his-spittle, his-slaver, because-of its-savouriness bird.
sentences.i: his mouth was watering, he was gaping, and his spittle and his slaver ran, for the savour of the bird.
sentences.n: Brasseur: 'au point que l'eau lui en venait à la bouche, qu'il en bâillait et que la salive et la bave lui découlaient'. cauahin 'it flows' (Brasseur gavahin) and cabiquilahic 'he gapes, yawns' (Brasseur gabiquilahic) keep Ximénez's plain c; both inferred. vvaal 'its liquid', the water of his mouth (inferred). pu chi 'in the mouth', chi 'mouth' (toggle chi'). vchub, vcaxah 'his spittle, his slaver' are a couplet; vcaxah keeps plain c where Brasseur has g (u gaxah). curulah 'run, drip' is inferred. vzimzohil 'its savouriness': zimzoh (zimizoh above) + -il.

sentences.t: Ta xuꜩonoh cut: “Naquipa ri iuecha? Quiꜩih cuz ruxlab ca nu nao. Chi ya ta zcaquin vech,” xcha cut.
sentences.l: Then he-asked then: “What the your(pl.)-food? Truly sweet(?) its-smell ongoing I perceive. You(pl.)-give (ta) a-little to-me,” he-said then.
sentences.i: Then he asked: “What is that food of yours? Truly sweet is the smell of it that comes to me. Give me a little,” he said.
sentences.n: xuꜩonoh 'he asked': x- + v- 'he' + ꜩonoh 'ask'. iuecha 'your (pl.) food': iv- + echa 'food', u for v. cuz 'sweet, savoury' (Brasseur guz, with g; plain c, printed as written), inferred. ca nu nao 'I perceive it': nao 'feel, know', with nu- 'I'. Chi ya ta 'give (pl.)': ch- + i- + ya 'give', with ta. vech 'to me': v- 'my' + ech, 'mine'.

sentences.t: Ta xya cut hun ꜩiquin chire Cabracan, vchacatahic curi.
sentences.l: Then was-given then one bird to-him Cabracan, his-being-brought-low then.
sentences.i: Then a bird was given to Cabracan, and that was his downfall.
sentences.n: xya 'it was given': ya 'give' with x-, no person marked; the passive sense is inferred (Brasseur 'on lui donna'). vchacatahic curi 'his bringing low, that': the bird is his overthrow.

sentences.t: Catecut xuquiz ri ꜩiquin, ta xbe chicut, xeopon cu chila relebal ꜫih, ꜭo vi ri nima huyub.
sentences.l: Then-then he-finished the bird, then he-went again-then, they-arrived then there its-going-out-place sun, is there the great mountain.
sentences.i: When he had finished the bird they set off again, and came there to where the sun comes out, where the great mountain is.
sentences.n: Catecut 'then', cate + cut as one word (toggle k'atek'ut). xuquiz 'he finished it': x- + v- 'he' + quiz 'end' (Brasseur x-u qiz, his q the letter of ꜭ; the toggle k'is, as xquiz). xbe 'he went' and xeopon 'they arrived', singular then plural, as at the start of the part.

sentences.t: Are curi Cabracan xa tubul chic racan vcab; mabi chi couin chic, rumal ri vleu xcul chirih ꜩiquin xutio.
sentences.l: This then Cabracan only weak(?) now his-leg his-hand; not that he-can any-more, because-of the earth was-coated on-its-back bird he-ate.
sentences.i: And now Cabracan's legs and arms were giving way; he no longer had any strength, because of the earth that had been smeared on the bird he ate.
sentences.n: tubul 'giving way, tottering' (inferred; Brasseur 'chancelant des pieds et des mains'). racan vcab 'his legs, his arms': vcab is 'his hand, his arm' here, cab 'hand' with plain c (Brasseur u gab), the toggle uq'ab'; it is not v cab 'the second' of the opening. mabi chi couin chic 'he could no longer': couin 'be able, have strength' (cou 'strong'); mabi is a form of maui 'not'. xcul 'it was smeared', the verb of xqui cul above. xutio 'he bit it, ate it': x- + v- + tio, the bite verb, its ti written with the ß-ligature (toggle ti'o, as in the earlier parts).

sentences.t: Ma cu habi chic naquila xu ban chic chire huyub; maui xuꜩinic xu vlih tah.
sentences.l: Not then there-was any-more anything he did again to mountain; not it-came-right he bring-down (tah).
sentences.i: There was nothing more that he could do to the mountains; he did not manage to bring them down.
sentences.n: Ma cu habi (MS macuhabi), xu ban chic (MS xubanchic) and xu vlih tah are divided as the established text has them. maui … tah 'not': the negative in two parts. xuꜩinic 'it came right, it succeeded' (vꜩin 'be complete'): he did not succeed in bringing them down.

sentences.t: Ta xim cut cumal ꜭaholab; chirih xim vi v cab;
sentences.l: Then he-was-tied then by-them boys; behind-him were-tied there his hand;
sentences.i: Then he was bound by the boys: his arms were bound behind his back;
sentences.n: xim 'he was tied': the root is xim 'tie, bind' (modern ximik), here passive, the x- of the completive not written apart (inferred; Brasseur 'ayant ensuite été lié'). chirih 'behind him, at his back'. v cab, written apart here, is 'his hand' (Brasseur u gab), as vcab in the last sentence, not v cab 'the second'; the toggle q'ab'.

sentences.t: xrilih vcab cumal ꜭaholab; xim cut vcul racan vcabichal.
sentences.l: it-was-watched(?) his-hand by-them boys; were-tied then his-neck his-leg together.
sentences.i: the boys kept watch on his arms; and his neck and his legs were tied together.
sentences.n: xrilih 'it was watched': il 'see, watch' with r- and -ih, after Brasseur ('gardées par les jeunes gens'); the form is not clear. vcul racan vcabichal, as Brasseur prints it (u cul rakan u cabichal): vcul 'his neck' (the modern qul 'neck', so the toggle uqul; Ximénez and Brasseur write c), racan 'his legs', vcabichal 'together, the two of them', cab 'two' + -ichal. It is the word left unexplained in the fifth part (qui cabichal); here it follows Brasseur ('ensemble').

sentences.t: Catecut xqui tarih cahoc puleu, xqui mucu.
sentences.l: Then-then they threw-him downward to-earth, they buried-him.
sentences.i: Then they threw him down to the ground, and they buried him.
sentences.n: xqui tarih 'they threw (him)': tarih 'let fall, throw' (inferred, as in the sixth part). xqui mucu 'they buried him' (Brasseur x-qui muku): muc 'bury' + -u, as muc above. puleu 'into the earth': so the boys did what they said over the roasting bird, on the earth, in the earth.

sentences.t: Quehecut vchacatahic Cabracan ri xavi xere Hunahpu, Xbalanque; maui ahilan qui banoh varal chuvach vleuh.
sentences.l: Thus-then his-being-brought-low Cabracan the just only-these Hunahpu, Xbalanque; not counted their doing here on-the-face-of earth.
sentences.i: Such was the downfall of Cabracan, by Hunahpu and Xbalanque alone; beyond counting are the things they did here on the face of the earth.
sentences.n: Quehecut 'thus then', quehe + cut as one word (toggle keje'k'ut). xavi xere 'just these, these alone', as when the episode began. ahilan 'counted' (ahil 'count', modern ajilaj, with -an; inferred): their deeds were not to be counted.

sentences.t: Are chicut xchi ca biyh chic calaxic Hunahpu, Xbalanque;
sentences.l: This again-then shall we tell now their-birth Hunahpu, Xbalanque;
sentences.i: Now we shall tell of the birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque;
sentences.n: calaxic 'their being born': al 'child' + -ax- (passive) + -ic, with c-, the form of qui 'their' before a vowel (Brasseur c' alaxic); inferred. The next part goes back a generation, to the boys' fathers.

sentences.t: are nabe mi xca biyh ri qui chacatahic Vvcub Caquix, ruc Zipacna, ruꜭ Cabracan, varal chuvach vleuh.
sentences.l: this first just-now we-told the their being-brought-low Seven Macaw, with Zipacna, with Cabracan, here on-the-face-of earth.
sentences.i: first we have told of the downfall of Vucub Caquix, with Zipacna, with Cabracan, here on the face of the earth.
sentences.n: mi xca biyh 'we have just told': mi 'just now' + xca 'we (did)' + biyh; the MS seems to have xcabißh, printed biyh as elsewhere. ruc … ruꜭ 'with': the same word twice in one line, first with plain c, then with the cuatrillo; both are printed as written, and the toggle gives ruk' for both, the word being certain. The three defeats are summed up, and the book turns from the sons of Vucub Caquix to the boys' own story.
